title: A lifetime mitochondria researcher says it may not drive normal aging
dek: Raising mitochondrial DNA mutations to 10 times normal aging didn't trigger aging in mice—suggesting that in healthy people, mitochondrial decline may be coincidental rather than causal.
why: The first half covers hard-core mechanism: electron transport chains and H2O2 signaling. The second half dissects metformin, urolithin A, NAD precursors, and hyperbaric oxygen one by one for target evidence. High information density but requires patience.
who: People skeptical of anti-aging supplements like metformin, NAD precursors, urolithin A, and hyperbaric oxygen who want mechanism evidence over marketing; and practitioners interested in mitochondrial biology fundamentals.
skip: The opening section on biochemical basics—superoxide dismutase, H2O2, antioxidants—can be skipped if you're already familiar with the electron transport chain.

points.h: Mitochondria's third function: signaling across the cell
points.body: Beyond producing ATP and synthesis precursors, mitochondria continuously signal the cell: leaked electrons generate H2O2 for immune cell differentiation; acetyl-CoA and α-ketoglutarate control histone acetylation and DNA demethylation; released mtDNA/RNA trigger interferon pathways. These three signaling pathways are independent of ATP production—the part rediscovered over the past 30 years.

points.h: Want to measure your mitochondrial function? No reliable method exists
points.body: Chandel says that aside from muscle biopsy, there's no way to assess mitochondrial function. Market tests using metabolomics or acylcarnitine ratios only measure steady-state concentrations at one moment, not flux—you can't distinguish whether elevated levels reflect a fast system, metabolite surplus, or blockage downstream.

points.h: With 70% redundancy, mitochondrial problems don't arise easily
points.body: Genetic evidence shows patients carrying mitochondrial mutations need 70% loss of mitochondrial protein function before cells malfunction—meaning mitochondria have enormous redundancy. Chandel's analogy: a car reaching 217 mph instead of 140 mph is irrelevant when the speed limit is 50 mph.

points.h: Mutating mitochondrial DNA doesn't replicate normal aging
points.body: Artificially mutating nuclear DNA in mice reproduces aging to some degree; but mutating mtDNA—even at 10 times normal aging rates—doesn't cause deterioration or aging-like phenotypes. This suggests mitochondrial dysfunction is *sufficient* to cause aging-like damage, but hasn't been proven *necessary* for normal aging.

points.h: Metformin works in the gut, not the liver
points.body: After oral ingestion, metformin reaches ~1 millimolar in intestinal cells, then drops to 50-100 micromolar entering the liver via the portal vein, and only ~10 micromolar in blood—a 20-fold drop. PET imaging with glucose shows signal concentrates in the gut, not liver; NDI1 protein experiments confirm that intestinal Complex I inhibition is the key mechanism.

points.h: Metformin's cancer trials failed because cells can't absorb it
points.body: Phase 3 trials for breast cancer and prostate cancer failed. In the lab, researchers identified a metformin-sensitive cancer cell line; once they knocked out the organic cation transporter (OCT) with CRISPR, that line became completely resistant. Most tumor tissues don't highly express these transporters—the drug can't reach them, likely explaining the trial failures.

points.h: Metformin fails against cancer but suppresses clonal hematopoiesis
points.body: Metformin doesn't target cancer, but suppresses clonal hematopoiesis. UK Biobank data on ~450,000 people shows lower rates of CHIP (age-related blood stem cell mutations that drive cardiovascular inflammation) in metformin users; three independent papers (two in Nature, one in Nature Communications) confirm that inhibiting Complex I blocks these clones, with metformin being the safest drug.

points.h: Hyperbaric oxygen has no evidence besides wound healing
points.body: Chandel advises against buying a hyperbaric oxygen chamber. ICU doctors want patients off high-oxygen as soon as possible—animal studies show prolonged hyperoxia causes lung epithelial cells to age and die. No benefit evidence exists. He sees the anti-aging popularity as largely sourced from an Israeli study measuring telomere length, but telomere length itself has weak evidence linking to lifespan.
